title: How Gender and Distance Impact Race Walking Speed
How Gender and Distance Impact Race Walking Speed
text:
The question
Competitive race walking was first introduced a few centuries ago in England. Its expansion interested us in finding how race distance and gender effect race walking speed. For this analysis, our target audience is competitive race walkers. Our hope is to help these racers optimize their racing times and speeds.
The data were gathered by the World Athletics Race Walking Team Championships. The full datset can be found outline through the following URL: https://data.scorenetwork.org/walking/racewalking_10k_20k_speeds_2024.html
Important variables in this dataset include gender, distance, and walking speed for each observational unit, the individual racer. These predictors enable us to recognize the relationships between each predictor and the response.

title: How Gender and Distance Impact Race Walking Speed
text:
What the baseline shows
We will use the multiple linear regression model because we have two or more variables (race distance and gender) to predict the outcome of our continuous response variable (speed). This model will allow us to see how the variables independently affect the outcome before adding the interaction.
Holding race distance constant, women have a predicted average race-walking speed of 27.96 meters/minute lower than men. One specific limitation is that race distance and gender don’t fully account for speed as there are underlying factors and covariates such as race-walking experience and age.


Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(readr)

racewalking <- read_csv("~/Downloads/racewalking.csv")

baseline <- lm(SPEED ~ DISTANCE + GENDER, data = racewalking)
summary(baseline)
